opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, and the answer is different depending on which company you're looking at.

On the surface, a lot of what Chinese labs are doing looks economically hard to justify. They're training large models, often releasing the weights openly, and they don't have the same paid enterprise API market that OpenAI or Anthropic have in the US. Chinese enterprises have historically been less willing to pay for software, and token prices there have been pushed down to almost nothing by price wars. So if you judge it purely as "sell model access, make a profit," it doesn't look sustainable for many of them.

But I don't think that's how most of them see it. For the big tech companies, Alibaba, ByteDance, Tencent, AI models are a strategic layer on top of businesses that already make lots of money: cloud, e-commerce, short video, gaming, advertising. A model like Qwen isn't a standalone product that has to pay for itself. It drives cloud adoption, it builds a developer ecosystem, and it keeps them relevant. Those companies can sustain this kind of spending for a long time, the same way Meta funded Llama out of its ad business.

The startups are more fragile. There were a lot of well-funded model companies a couple of years ago, and I think we've already seen consolidation, with some pivoting to applications or narrower verticals. That's healthy and expected. Not everyone can stay at the frontier, because frontier training keeps getting more expensive.

DeepSeek is its own interesting case, since it's backed by a quant fund and doesn't need to raise money in the usual way. That gives it a lot of freedom to focus on research and openness without short-term commercial pressure.

Then there's the compute constraint. Export controls mean Chinese labs have less access to the top Nvidia chips, which has forced them to be very efficient, and honestly some of the most impressive engineering in the field has come out of that. But over the long run, compute access still matters a lot, and domestic chips are improving but not at parity yet. So I'd say the question isn't only whether they can afford it financially. It's also whether they can get enough compute to keep up as scaling continues.

There's also a national-strategy element. AI is seen in China as critical infrastructure, so there's policy support and a sense that having strong domestic models is non-negotiable. That changes the calculation. It's less "is this profitable this year" and more "can we afford not to do this."

So my overall view: the big players are sustainable because AI is subsidized by existing businesses and national priorities, a few research-focused labs are sustainable because of unusual funding structures, and many of the pure-play startups will struggle. And the open-weight strategy is a deliberate choice. It wins mindshare and adoption globally, which is a form of value even if it doesn't show up immediately as revenue.

r001.rationale: The response says major tech companies can sustain the spending, but also says many pure-play startups will struggle. It does not judge Chinese companies’ current spending as generally within their financial means.

r002.rationale: It notes that some startups have already consolidated or pivoted, but does not predict eventual market consolidation conditional on model capabilities continuing to improve.

r003.rationale: It says frontier training is getting more expensive, but does not state that additional investment yields diminishing gains in model capability.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention Ant Bailing or attribute its team formation to redeployed existing talent.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's more sustainable than a lot of people in the US want to believe, but the sustainability looks really different depending on which company you're talking about.

If you look at the big players, the Alibabas and the ByteDances, the Tencents, these are companies with enormous cash flows from businesses that have nothing to do with AI. For them, training a frontier-ish model is a rounding error. Alibaba's Qwen team has been shipping open models at a pace that frankly embarrasses a lot of Western labs, and they can keep doing that for a very long time because the capex is tiny relative to the parent company. So that tier, I'm not worried about at all.

Where it gets more interesting is the smaller labs, the ones people call the "AI tigers," and then something like DeepSeek, which is a bit of its own animal because it's funded by a quant hedge fund and doesn't really have the same pressure to monetize. DeepSeek showed that you can be remarkably compute-efficient, and that changed the conversation. But the flip side is that compute is still the binding constraint. Export controls are real. When your access to the best Nvidia chips is uncertain, you're forced into a strategy of efficiency and open weights, because you can't win on raw scale and you can't easily sell a closed API globally. Open weights become the distribution strategy, and that's what we're seeing.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that this is some kind of state-directed, bottomless-money situation. A lot of these labs are operating under real financial pressure. Some of the tiger startups have already pivoted away from pretraining toward applications because they couldn't justify the spend. That's actually a sign of a functioning market, not a sign of collapse.

So my take is: the top layer is durable, the middle is consolidating fast, and the whole ecosystem is going to keep being the primary source of strong open models for the foreseeable future. If anything, the question I'd flip back is whether American companies can sustain the pace of giving things away, because right now China is winning the open ecosystem by default, and I don't think that's where the US wants to be.

r001.rationale: The response says major firms can easily afford model development, but also says smaller labs face real financial pressure and some could not justify continued pretraining. It does not judge Chinese companies’ current spending overall to be within their means.

r002.rationale: It says the middle is consolidating fast, but does not predict eventual market consolidation conditional on model capabilities continuing to improve.

r003.rationale: The response discusses compute efficiency, but does not say that additional investment yields diminishing gains in model capability.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention Ant Bailing or attribute a large-model team’s rapid formation to redeployed existing talent.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by sustainability. Training a competitive model is one thing; building a business that can fund the next generation of models is another. That distinction applies to Chinese companies just as much as it does to American companies.

For a company with a large existing business, investing in its own models can make sense even if selling access to the model isn’t profitable on its own. The value might come from improving its products, lowering costs, or having more control over technology it considers essential. For a startup that has to recover all of its training costs through API revenue, the economics are much harder, especially when prices keep falling.

There’s also the question of access to compute. If getting chips is more difficult, that creates a real constraint on how often you can run large experiments. Efficiency helps, but it doesn’t make that constraint disappear.

So I wouldn’t expect every company building models today to keep doing it indefinitely. But I also wouldn’t conclude that Chinese investment in models is inherently unsustainable. The key question is whether a company has a durable reason to own the model—and a business that can support that investment over multiple generations.

r001.rationale: The response discusses sustainability in general and says economics vary by company, but does not judge whether Chinese companies’ current model-development spending is within their financial means.

r002.rationale: It does not predict consolidation of the AI model market as capabilities improve.

r003.rationale: It mentions that efficiency helps with compute constraints, but does not state that additional model-development investment yields diminishing capability gains.

r004.rationale: It does not mention Ant Bailing or explain its team formation through redeployed existing talent.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what they’re trying to get out of building their own models. If you’re a large company and AI is going to be a core part of your products, there’s a strategic reason to invest. You gain control over costs, how the model behaves, and how closely it fits your business. You don’t necessarily need to have the best model in the world for that investment to make sense.

The harder question is whether everyone can sustain the race to train the next frontier model. That requires ongoing spending on compute, researchers, and experimentation. Having enough money for one training run is very different from having a business that can support that process for years.

So I would look at whether these companies are turning model development into useful products and revenue. If the model improves an existing business, there’s a plausible path to sustainability. If the entire strategy is just to keep climbing the benchmarks and figure out the business later, I’d be much more skeptical. I’d expect some consolidation, alongside companies finding narrower areas where owning a model really pays off.

r001.rationale: The response discusses when model investment may be sustainable, but does not judge Chinese companies’ current spending as being within their financial means.

r002.rationale: It expects “some consolidation,” but does not connect that prediction to continued capability improvements or say that the market will probably eventually consolidate.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that further model-development investment yields diminishing gains in capability.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention Ant Bailing or explain its team’s formation through redeployed existing talent.
